passages.title: Rawls, Utilitarianism and Justice Between Generations
passages.passage: Utilitarianism, associated with Jeremy Bentham and J.S. Mill, holds that a law or action is right in so far as it promotes the greatest happiness of the greatest number; Bentham's 'felicific calculus' sought to measure pleasure and pain by their intensity, duration and certainty. Critics object that the principle can justify sacrificing a minority for the benefit of the majority. John Rawls, in A Theory of Justice (1971), answered with 'justice as fairness'. The principles of justice, he argued, are those which free and rational persons would choose in an 'original position' behind a 'veil of ignorance', where no one knows his class, talents or even the generation to which he belongs. Two principles emerge. The first guarantees equal basic liberties for all and has lexical priority over the second. The second permits social and economic inequalities only if they are attached to positions open to all under fair equality of opportunity and work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged, which is the 'difference principle'. Because the parties do not know their generation, Rawls added a 'just savings principle': each generation must put aside a fair amount of capital and resources for those that follow. Robert Nozick, in Anarchy, State and Utopia, rejected such patterned theories and defended an entitlement theory, under which a distribution is just if holdings were justly acquired and justly transferred, which supports only a minimal State. Amartya Sen's capability approach, in The Idea of Justice, shifts attention from the holding of primary goods, on which Rawls relied, to what persons are actually able to do and to be. The Brundtland Commission's report, Our Common Future (1987), defined sustainable development as development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs, a formulation widely described as a principle of intergenerational equity, which Indian courts have invoked in environmental cases.

questions.question: The 'veil of ignorance' in Rawls's theory is designed to ensure that the parties who choose the principles of justice

options.A: decide by applying the greatest-happiness calculation of the majority
options.B: know their own talents and bargain for the greatest personal advantage
options.C: are bound by the commands of a sovereign who fixes the outcome
options.D: do not know their own class, talents or generation, and therefore choose impartially

questions.explanation: The veil removes knowledge of particular advantages, so that the principles chosen are impartial.

questions.question: According to the passage, an inequality is permissible in Rawls's scheme only if it

options.A: arises from just acquisition and transfer, whatever its effect on the poor
options.B: is approved by a majority of citizens in a vote
options.C: attaches to positions open to all under fair equality of opportunity and works to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged
options.D: increases total happiness even where the least advantaged are made worse off

questions.explanation: This is the second principle together with the difference principle.

questions.question: Which of the following best links Rawls's 'just savings principle' with the Brundtland definition of sustainable development?

options.A: Both allow the present generation to consume freely so long as current welfare is maximised
options.B: Both require the present generation to take account of the claims of future generations in the use of resources and capital
options.C: Both treat the interests of future generations as irrelevant until those generations exist
options.D: Both are derived from Nozick's entitlement theory

questions.explanation: Each imposes a duty of fairness across generations, which is the core of intergenerational equity.

questions.question: A mining project promises large revenue to the present generation but will permanently exhaust an aquifer on which a tribal community and later generations depend. Which objection is most consistent with Rawls's theory?

options.A: Its effect on happiness cannot be measured by a felicific calculus
options.B: It worsens the position of the least advantaged and breaches the duty to save for later generations
options.C: It interferes with entitlements acquired by the mining company through just transfer
options.D: It has not been approved by a majority of present voters

questions.explanation: The difference principle and the just savings principle together condemn the project; the other options reflect other theories or irrelevant tests.

questions.question: Consider the following statements. 1. Bentham's felicific calculus measures pleasure and pain by intensity, duration and certainty. 2. In Rawls's theory, the principle of equal basic liberties has lexical priority over the second principle. 3. Nozick defends the difference principle as a requirement of justice. Which of the statements are correct?

options.A: 1 and 2 only
options.B: 1 and 3 only
options.C: 2 and 3 only
options.D: 1, 2 and 3

questions.explanation: Statements 1 and 2 appear in the passage; Nozick rejects patterned principles such as the difference principle.

questions.question: Assertion (A): Sen's capability approach differs from Rawls's emphasis on the distribution of primary goods. Reason (R): Sen directs attention to what persons are actually able to do and to be. Which is correct?

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: R states precisely how Sen departs from Rawls, and so explains A.

passages.title: Feminist Jurisprudence and the Idea of Substantive Equality
passages.passage: Feminist jurisprudence examines how law constructs and entrenches gender hierarchy. Liberal feminism seeks formal equality: women should be treated as men are, and sex-based classifications should be removed. Difference or 'cultural' feminism, associated with Carol Gilligan's In a Different Voice, contends that women often reason from an ethic of care and relationship rather than abstract rights, and that law should accommodate that difference. Catharine MacKinnon's dominance approach regards gender as a hierarchy of power and asks not whether women are treated the same as or differently from men, but whether law perpetuates the subordination of women. Kimberle Crenshaw coined the term 'intersectionality' to describe how discrimination on grounds such as race, caste and sex combines, so that the experience of a person subject to several grounds cannot be understood by examining each ground separately. Indian constitutional law reflects these debates. Article 15(1) prohibits discrimination on grounds only of sex, but Article 15(3) permits special provisions for women and children. In Anuj Garg v. Hotel Association of India (2007), the Supreme Court struck down a law prohibiting the employment of women in establishments serving liquor, holding that protective laws founded on stereotypes of women's vulnerability restrict their autonomy, and that protection must not become a pretext for exclusion. In Githa Hariharan v. Reserve Bank of India (1999), the Court read the word 'after' in Section 6(a) of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act as 'in the absence of', so that a mother may act as natural guardian even while the father is alive. In Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018), the Court struck down Section 497 of the Indian Penal Code, which treated the wife as the property of her husband, for violating Articles 14, 15 and 21. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 contains no offence corresponding to Section 497. The Court has repeatedly said that substantive equality requires attention to the real conditions of women's lives.

questions.question: Liberal feminism, as described in the passage, is chiefly concerned to secure

options.A: separate legal systems for women
options.B: formal equality, so that women are treated as men are and sex-based classifications are removed
options.C: an ethic of care which the law should adopt in place of rights
options.D: recognition that gender is a hierarchy of power

questions.explanation: The passage identifies formal equality as the liberal feminist goal.

questions.question: MacKinnon's dominance approach asks whether

options.A: women reason differently from men
options.B: discrimination was intended by the legislature
options.C: the law perpetuates the subordination of women
options.D: women are treated identically with men in every respect

questions.explanation: The test is dominance and subordination, not sameness or difference.

questions.question: A Dalit woman worker is denied promotion. The employer shows that Dalit men and upper-caste women in the same unit have been promoted, and argues that there is no discrimination on either ground. The concept that best explains why a single-ground analysis may fail to capture her claim is

options.A: the ethic of care
options.B: intersectionality
options.C: formal equality
options.D: protective discrimination under Article 15(3)

questions.explanation: Intersectionality addresses the combined effect of caste and sex, which separate comparisons miss.

questions.question: The Court struck down the restriction on women's employment in Anuj Garg because

options.A: Article 15(3) forbids any special provision for women
options.B: Parliament alone had competence to regulate such employment
options.C: protective laws founded on stereotypes restrict women's autonomy and cannot be justified as protection
options.D: the liquor trade is an absolute fundamental right

questions.explanation: The passage records the reasoning that paternalistic, stereotype-based protection restricts autonomy.

questions.question: Consider the following statements. 1. In Joseph Shine v. Union of India, the Supreme Court struck down Section 497 of the Indian Penal Code. 2. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 retains an offence corresponding to Section 497. 3. In Githa Hariharan, the Court read 'after' in Section 6(a) of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act as 'in the absence of'. Which of the statements are correct?

options.A: 1 and 2 only
options.B: 1 and 3 only
options.C: 2 and 3 only
options.D: 1, 2 and 3

questions.explanation: Statements 1 and 3 are stated in the passage; the BNS has no corresponding offence.

questions.question: Which proposition is most consistent with the passage regarding Article 15(3)?

options.A: Article 15(3) applies only to children
options.B: Article 15(3) overrides Article 15(1) in every case
options.C: Article 15(3) authorises the complete exclusion of women from any occupation
options.D: Special provisions for women are permitted, but those founded on stereotypes of vulnerability may fail scrutiny

questions.explanation: Anuj Garg shows that Article 15(3) does not validate stereotype-driven exclusion.

passages.title: Sustainable Development: Balance, Burden and Non-Regression
passages.passage: The Brundtland Commission defined sustainable development as development that meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs. The non-binding Rio Declaration of 1992 elaborates the idea: Principle 3 requires that the right to development be fulfilled so as to meet equitably the developmental and environmental needs of present and future generations, Principle 4 makes environmental protection an integral part of development, Principle 15 states the precautionary approach, and Principle 16 says that the polluter should, in principle, bear the cost of pollution. Indian courts, drawing on Articles 21, 48A and 51A(g), have made these ideas part of domestic law. In Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum (1996), the precautionary and polluter pays principles were accepted as essential features of sustainable development. In A.P. Pollution Control Board v. M.V. Nayudu (1999), the Court held that, where the effects of an activity are uncertain, the burden of showing that it is environmentally benign lies on its proponent, and stressed the need for expert environmental authorities. In Narmada Bachao Andolan v. Union of India (2000), the majority declined to halt the Sardar Sarovar project, holding that development and environment must be balanced and that a project may proceed where adequate environmental and rehabilitation safeguards are in place. In Intellectuals Forum, Tirupathi v. State of A.P. (2006), the Court invoked intergenerational equity and the public trust to protect water bodies. In Hanuman Laxman Aroskar v. Union of India (2019), the Court set aside an environmental clearance for an airport in Goa for want of a cumulative impact assessment and recognised the principle of non-regression: standards of environmental protection, once attained, should not be diluted without compelling justification. In Harbinder Singh Sekhon v. State of Punjab (February 2026), the Court held that a dilution of preventive environmental safeguards, without proportionate and scientifically substantiated justification, is arbitrary and infringes the right to a clean environment under Article 21.

questions.question: The 'principle of non-regression' recognised in Aroskar means that

options.A: standards of environmental protection once attained should not be diluted without compelling justification
options.B: a project once cleared can never be reviewed
options.C: developing States may not reduce their emissions
options.D: polluters are exempt from liability after a clearance

questions.explanation: The passage states the principle in these terms.

questions.question: A State amends its rules to halve the mandatory buffer zone around industrial units, without any scientific study, to attract investment. In the light of the passage, the amendment is

options.A: invalid only if Parliament has passed a contrary law
options.B: valid, since the right to development always prevails
options.C: valid, since the Rio Declaration is binding on the State
options.D: open to challenge as arbitrary, since dilution of preventive safeguards needs proportionate, reasoned and scientific justification

questions.explanation: Harbinder Singh Sekhon (2026) condemns unjustified dilution as arbitrary and contrary to Article 21.

questions.question: The approach of the majority in Narmada Bachao Andolan, as described in the passage, was that

options.A: development always prevails over environmental concerns
options.B: courts must decide the technical merits of dam design
options.C: development and environment must be balanced, and a project may proceed where adequate safeguards are in place
options.D: environmental concerns always prevail over development

questions.explanation: The majority accepted the project with safeguards, on a balancing approach.

questions.question: In Nayudu, where the effects of an activity on the environment are uncertain, the burden of proof is on

options.A: the court
options.B: the citizen who objects to it
options.C: the person proposing the activity
options.D: the pollution control board in every case

questions.explanation: The precautionary principle shifts the burden to the proponent.

questions.question: Assertion (A): The principle of intergenerational equity restricts the freedom of the present generation in the use of natural resources. Reason (R): The Brundtland formulation requires present needs to be met without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs. Which is correct?

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: R states the content of the principle that justifies the restriction in A.

questions.question: Consider the following statements. 1. Principle 16 of the Rio Declaration states that the polluter should, in principle, bear the cost of pollution. 2. Principle 15 of the Rio Declaration states the precautionary approach. 3. The Rio Declaration is a binding treaty which Indian courts must enforce as such. Which of the statements are correct?

options.A: 1 and 2 only
options.B: 1 and 3 only
options.C: 2 and 3 only
options.D: 1, 2 and 3

questions.explanation: Statements 1 and 2 are accurate; the Declaration is non-binding and its principles operate in India through domestic law and judicial recognition.

passages.title: Environmental Clearance and the Fate of Ex Post Facto Approvals
passages.passage: The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 authorises the Central Government under Section 3 to take all measures necessary to protect and improve the environment. The EIA Notification, 2006, issued under that power, requires prior environmental clearance (EC) for listed projects. Category A projects are appraised at the Centre by an Expert Appraisal Committee, and Category B projects at the State level by the State Environment Impact Assessment Authority. The process has four stages: screening, scoping, public consultation and appraisal. A project may not be commenced, other than for limited preliminary work, before the EC is granted. In Common Cause v. Union of India (2017) and Alembic Pharmaceuticals v. Rohit Prajapati (2020), the Supreme Court described ex post facto clearance, that is, clearance granted after a project has begun or operated without prior EC, as alien to environmental jurisprudence. A 2017 notification created a one-time window for violators to apply for ex post facto EC, and a 2021 Office Memorandum provided a continuing mechanism. In Vanashakti v. Union of India (16 May 2025), a two-judge Bench struck down both and barred such clearances in future. On 18 November 2025, a three-judge Bench, by a majority of two to one, recalled that judgment, reasoning that Common Cause had not laid down an absolute bar and that the demolition of completed projects would waste valuable public resources; Justice Bhuyan dissented, holding that the concept is contrary to the precautionary principle. In 2026, in the review proceedings, the Court held that the prior EC regime under the 2006 Notification is mandatory and does not admit post facto clearance without formal amendment. It invalidated the continuing 2021 Office Memorandum but upheld the Centre's power under Section 3 of the 1986 Act to frame tailored amnesty schemes for violators.

questions.question: Under the EIA Notification, 2006, as described in the passage, Category A projects are appraised by

options.A: the State Environment Impact Assessment Authority
options.B: an Expert Appraisal Committee at the Centre
options.C: the Gram Sabha
options.D: the National Green Tribunal

questions.explanation: The passage assigns Category A to the Centre and Category B to the State authority.

questions.question: An 'ex post facto' environmental clearance is one granted

options.A: only for Category B projects
options.B: after a public hearing has been held
options.C: after the project has begun or operated without prior clearance
options.D: before the project report is prepared

questions.explanation: The passage defines the term in these words.

questions.question: In the November 2025 recall of the Vanashakti judgment, the majority reasoned that

options.A: the Supreme Court has no power to review its own judgments
options.B: the 2006 Notification itself permits post facto clearance in every case
options.C: the precautionary principle does not apply to clearances
options.D: Common Cause had not laid down an absolute bar, and demolition of completed projects would waste public resources

questions.explanation: The passage records these two reasons.

questions.question: Which executive measure is most consistent with the Court's 2026 holding on ex post facto clearance?

options.A: An order treating prior EC as optional for Category B projects
options.B: A tailored, one-time amnesty scheme for violators framed under Section 3 of the 1986 Act
options.C: A permanent Office Memorandum allowing any violator to seek regularisation at any time
options.D: A rule permitting commencement of construction before EC for Category A projects

questions.explanation: The Court invalidated the continuing Office Memorandum but upheld the power to frame tailored amnesty schemes.

questions.question: Consider the following statements. 1. Prior environmental clearance is mandatory under the 2006 Notification, according to the Court's 2026 holding. 2. The May 2025 Vanashakti judgment was recalled by a majority of two to one. 3. Justice Bhuyan agreed with the majority in the November 2025 recall. Which of the statements are correct?

options.A: 1 and 2 only
options.B: 1 and 3 only
options.C: 2 and 3 only
options.D: 1, 2 and 3

questions.explanation: Statements 1 and 2 are correct; Justice Bhuyan dissented.

questions.question: Assertion (A): Justice Bhuyan regarded ex post facto clearance as contrary to the precautionary principle. Reason (R): Prior assessment of impact is the essence of the precautionary approach, whereas post facto assessment examines harm after it has occurred. Which is correct?

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: R gives the reasoning which supports A.

passages.title: Climate Law: The Paris Agreement and India's Domestic Architecture
passages.passage: Article 2(1)(a) of the Paris Agreement (2015) aims to hold the increase in global average temperature well below 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5 degrees. Under Article 4, each Party must prepare, communicate and maintain successive nationally determined contributions (NDCs) reflecting progression over time. The Agreement is to be implemented to reflect equity and the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities (CBDR-RC), in the light of different national circumstances, which means that all States share responsibility but the obligations differ according to historical contribution and capacity. Article 6 allows voluntary cooperative approaches, including the use of internationally transferred mitigation outcomes, and establishes a mechanism for trading emission reductions. At the Glasgow summit in 2021, India announced the goal of net-zero emissions by 2070. India's updated NDC (2022) commits to reducing the emissions intensity of its GDP by 45 per cent by 2030 from the 2005 level, and to achieving about 50 per cent cumulative electric power installed capacity from non-fossil sources by 2030, subject to technology transfer and low-cost climate finance. India has no single comprehensive climate statute; its response rests on sectoral laws such as the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and the Energy Conservation Act, 2001. The Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act, 2022 empowers the Centre to specify a carbon credit trading scheme and to require designated consumers to use a minimum share of non-fossil energy. The Green Credit Programme (2023), notified under the 1986 Act, is a voluntary, market-based mechanism that rewards environmentally positive actions such as afforestation and water conservation. In M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India (2024), the Supreme Court read Articles 14 and 21 to include a right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change, giving a constitutional dimension to climate protection in the absence of a general statute.

questions.question: The temperature goal in Article 2(1)(a) of the Paris Agreement is to hold the increase well below

options.A: 2.5 degrees Celsius, with 2 degrees as a stretch target
options.B: 1 degree Celsius above the 2005 level
options.C: 3 degrees Celsius, with no further effort
options.D: 2 degrees Celsius, while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5 degrees

questions.explanation: The passage states the goal in these terms.

questions.question: The principle of CBDR-RC means that

options.A: developing States are exempt from submitting NDCs
options.B: all States share responsibility for climate change, but their obligations differ according to historical contribution and capacity
options.C: all States must reduce emissions by an identical percentage
options.D: only developed States have obligations under the Agreement

questions.explanation: The passage explains the principle in these terms.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes India's domestic climate architecture on the basis of the passage?

options.A: India has enacted a Climate Change Act that creates a mandatory national carbon tax
options.B: India's NDC is a statute enforceable in the High Courts
options.C: India has no single comprehensive climate statute and relies on sectoral laws such as the 1986 Act and the Energy Conservation Act, as amended
options.D: India's climate response is codified wholly in the Energy Conservation Act, 2001

questions.explanation: The passage states that there is no single comprehensive climate statute.

questions.question: The use of internationally transferred mitigation outcomes is provided for in

options.A: Article 2(1)(a) of the Paris Agreement
options.B: Section 3 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986
options.C: the Green Credit Programme of 2023
options.D: Article 6 of the Paris Agreement

questions.explanation: Article 6 provides for voluntary cooperative approaches, including transferred mitigation outcomes.

questions.question: The Green Credit Programme, 2023 is best described as

options.A: a compulsory tax on all industrial emissions
options.B: a replacement for the carbon credit trading scheme under the Energy Conservation Act
options.C: a voluntary, market-based mechanism rewarding environmentally positive actions such as afforestation and water conservation
options.D: a treaty obligation under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement

questions.explanation: The passage describes it as voluntary and market-based.

questions.question: Assertion (A): The decision in M.K. Ranjitsinh gives climate protection a constitutional footing in India even though there is no comprehensive climate statute. Reason (R): The Court read Articles 14 and 21 to include a right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change. Which is correct?

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: R states the basis for the constitutional recognition asserted in A.

passages.title: Transboundary Harm, Climate Obligations and the Oceans
passages.passage: The principle that a State must not allow its territory to be used to harm others has deep roots. In the Trail Smelter arbitration (United States v. Canada, 1941), the tribunal held that, under the principles of international law, no State has the right to use or permit the use of its territory so as to cause injury by fumes in or to the territory of another, where the case is of serious consequence and the injury is established by clear and convincing evidence. Principle 21 of the Stockholm Declaration (1972) and Principle 2 of the Rio Declaration (1992) affirm the sovereign right of States to exploit their resources under their own environmental and developmental policies, together with the responsibility to ensure that activities within their jurisdiction do not damage the environment of other States or of areas beyond national jurisdiction. In Pulp Mills on the River Uruguay (Argentina v. Uruguay, 2010), the International Court of Justice held that, where a proposed industrial activity may have a significant adverse impact in a transboundary context, an environmental impact assessment is a requirement under general international law, the content of which is left to each State's domestic law. In Costa Rica v. Nicaragua (compensation, 2018), the Court held that compensation is due for damage to the environment itself, including the loss of goods and services which the damaged environment would have provided. In May 2024, the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, in an advisory opinion, held that anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions constitute pollution of the marine environment under UNCLOS, and that States must take all necessary measures to prevent, reduce and control it, the standard of due diligence being stringent in view of the risk. The Agreement on Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction (the High Seas Treaty), adopted in 2023, entered into force on 17 January 2026, 120 days after the sixtieth ratification. It provides for benefit-sharing from marine genetic resources, area-based management tools including marine protected areas, environmental impact assessments and capacity building. States that are not Parties may attend its Conference of the Parties only as observers. By contrast, negotiations in Geneva in August 2025 on a global treaty on plastic pollution ended without agreement.

questions.question: The Trail Smelter arbitration is regarded as the foundation of the rule that

options.A: a State has unlimited sovereignty over its natural resources
options.B: only treaties can create environmental obligations
options.C: pollution is a matter of exclusive domestic jurisdiction
options.D: a State may not allow its territory to be used so as to cause serious injury to the territory of another State

questions.explanation: The passage records the tribunal's statement of the no-harm principle.

questions.question: According to Pulp Mills, an environmental impact assessment is required where

options.A: a proposed activity risks a significant adverse transboundary impact, its content being determined by domestic law
options.B: a State proposes any industrial activity whatsoever
options.C: the neighbouring State consents to the activity
options.D: a treaty expressly requires it, and not otherwise

questions.explanation: The Court treated EIA as a requirement of general international law in such cases.

questions.question: In Costa Rica v. Nicaragua (2018), the International Court of Justice held that

options.A: compensation is available only for damage to private property
options.B: environmental damage can never be compensated in money
options.C: only the State in whose territory the harm occurs may claim restitution
options.D: compensation is due for damage to the environment itself, including loss of the goods and services the environment would have provided

questions.explanation: The passage states this holding.

questions.question: In its 2024 advisory opinion, the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea held that greenhouse gas emissions

options.A: constitute marine pollution under UNCLOS, which States must take all necessary measures to prevent, reduce and control
options.B: may be regulated only by the International Court of Justice
options.C: fall outside UNCLOS because they originate on land
options.D: are regulated only by the Paris Agreement and not by UNCLOS

questions.explanation: The passage records this holding.

questions.question: State X has not ratified the High Seas Treaty. On the basis of the passage, State X

options.A: may vote at the Conference of the Parties
options.B: is bound because the treaty has entered into force
options.C: must submit its marine activities to the International Court of Justice for review
options.D: is not bound by the Agreement as a treaty, and may attend its Conference of the Parties only as an observer

questions.explanation: A treaty binds only its Parties; non-Parties are observers at the Conference of the Parties.

questions.question: Consider the following statements. 1. Principle 2 of the Rio Declaration couples a State's sovereign right to exploit its resources with a responsibility not to damage the environment of other States. 2. In Costa Rica v. Nicaragua, the International Court of Justice held that compensation cannot be awarded for damage to the environment as such. 3. Negotiations in Geneva in August 2025 on a plastics treaty ended without agreement. Which of the statements are correct?

options.A: 1 and 2 only
options.B: 1 and 3 only
options.C: 2 and 3 only
options.D: 1, 2 and 3

questions.explanation: Statements 1 and 3 are stated in the passage; statement 2 contradicts the 2018 holding.

passages.title: Pollution Control Statutes and the National Green Tribunal
passages.passage: The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 and the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 create the Central and State Pollution Control Boards, which grant consent to establish and operate industries and may issue closure directions. Parliament has since decriminalised many offences. The Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023 replaced imprisonment for contravention of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 with a monetary penalty of not less than Rs 10,000, extendable to Rs 15 lakh, imposed by an adjudicating officer, and the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Amendment Act, 2024 adopted a similar approach. Critics fear that deterrence has been weakened, while the Government regards the change as a way of reducing the burden of litigation. The National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 established the Tribunal for the effective and expeditious disposal of cases relating to environmental protection. Under Section 14, the Tribunal hears civil cases involving a substantial question relating to the environment which arise out of the enactments listed in Schedule I: the Water Act, the Water Cess Act, the Forest (Conservation) Act, the Air Act, the Environment (Protection) Act, the Public Liability Insurance Act and the Biological Diversity Act. The Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 and the Indian Forest Act, 1927 are not in the Schedule. An application under Section 14 must be made within six months of the cause of action, extendable by up to sixty days, whereas an application for compensation under Section 15 may be made within five years. Under Section 20, the Tribunal must apply the principles of sustainable development, the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle. It is not bound by the Code of Civil Procedure or the law of evidence, but is guided by principles of natural justice, and an appeal against its orders lies to the Supreme Court within ninety days (Section 22). In Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai v. Ankita Sinha (2021), the Supreme Court held that the Tribunal may take cognisance of environmental issues suo motu, since its role is wider than that of a body deciding only disputes between parties.

questions.question: An appeal against an order of the National Green Tribunal lies to the Supreme Court within

options.A: one year
options.B: thirty days
options.C: ninety days
options.D: sixty days

questions.explanation: Section 22 provides for an appeal within ninety days.

questions.question: Which of the following enactments is NOT listed in Schedule I to the National Green Tribunal Act, as described in the passage?

options.A: The Indian Forest Act, 1927
options.B: The Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991
options.C: The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981
options.D: The Biological Diversity Act, 2002

questions.explanation: The passage states that the Wild Life (Protection) Act and the Indian Forest Act are outside the Schedule.

questions.question: The effect of the Jan Vishwas Act, 2023 on the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, as described in the passage, was to

options.A: abolish the Pollution Control Boards
options.B: transfer all environmental offences to the Supreme Court
options.C: increase the term of imprisonment for contravention
options.D: replace imprisonment for contravention with a monetary penalty of Rs 10,000 to Rs 15 lakh imposed by an adjudicating officer

questions.explanation: The passage records this change.

questions.question: In Ankita Sinha, the Supreme Court held that the National Green Tribunal

options.A: may take cognisance of environmental issues suo motu
options.B: has no power to act except on the application of a party
options.C: is bound strictly by the Code of Civil Procedure
options.D: may decide only criminal matters

questions.explanation: The passage states this holding.

questions.question: Residents discover on 1 January 2022 that a factory has contaminated their groundwater. On 1 December 2024 they apply to the Tribunal for compensation under Section 15. On the passage, the application is

options.A: barred, since it was not made within six months and sixty days
options.B: within the time allowed, since compensation applications may be made within five years
options.C: maintainable only before a civil court
options.D: barred, since appeals lie only within ninety days

questions.explanation: Section 15 allows five years; the six-month period applies to Section 14 applications.

questions.question: Consider the following statements. 1. The National Green Tribunal is bound strictly by the Code of Civil Procedure and the law of evidence. 2. The Tribunal must apply the principles of sustainable development, precaution and polluter pays. 3. The Supreme Court has recognised the Tribunal's power to act suo motu. Which of the statements are correct?

options.A: 1 and 2 only
options.B: 1 and 3 only
options.C: 2 and 3 only
options.D: 1, 2 and 3

questions.explanation: Statements 2 and 3 are correct; the Tribunal is guided by natural justice and is not strictly bound by the Code or evidence law.

passages.title: Wildlife, Biodiversity and Eco-sensitive Zones
passages.passage: The Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022 reduced the number of Schedules from six to four: Schedules I and II for specially protected animals, Schedule III for protected plants, and a new Schedule IV for specimens listed in the Appendices to the CITES Convention. The Schedule for vermin was omitted. The Act empowers the Central Government to regulate or prohibit the import, trade, possession and proliferation of invasive alien species, and it permits the owner of a captive elephant to transfer or transport it for religious or other purposes. The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 gives effect to the Convention on Biological Diversity through a three-tier structure: the National Biodiversity Authority, State Biodiversity Boards and local Biodiversity Management Committees, which prepare People's Biodiversity Registers. Foreign nationals and entities need approval for access to biological resources, and a person seeking an intellectual property right for an invention based on biological resources obtained from India needs the prior approval of the Authority. Benefit-sharing is a central feature. The Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act, 2023 decriminalised several offences by replacing imprisonment with monetary penalties, exempted AYUSH practitioners and the use of codified traditional knowledge from benefit-sharing, and allowed faster approvals for research; critics argue that it weakens community control. Judicial intervention has also been prominent. In Common Cause v. Union of India (2020), the Supreme Court permitted the introduction of African cheetahs into India on an experimental basis under the supervision of an expert committee. In T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad (June 2022), the Court directed a minimum one-kilometre eco-sensitive zone around every protected area. In April 2023 it modified that direction, holding that it need not apply where an eco-sensitive zone had already been prescribed or proposed, while retaining the prohibition on mining within national parks and sanctuaries. These developments reflect a continuing tension between conservation and development.

questions.question: The three-tier structure under the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 consists of

options.A: the National Green Tribunal, High Courts and Gram Sabhas
options.B: the Ministry of Environment, State Forest Departments and Municipal Corporations
options.C: the National Biodiversity Authority, State Biodiversity Boards and Biodiversity Management Committees
options.D: the Central Pollution Control Board, State Boards and District Magistrates

questions.explanation: The passage states the three tiers.

questions.question: The Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022 changed the Schedules by

options.A: abolishing the protection of plants
options.B: increasing them from four to six
options.C: creating a separate Schedule for vermin
options.D: reducing them from six to four and adding a Schedule for CITES-listed specimens

questions.explanation: The passage describes the reduction and the new Schedule IV.

questions.question: The Supreme Court's April 2023 modification of its eco-sensitive zone direction held that

options.A: the eco-sensitive zone requirement was withdrawn altogether, including the ban on mining
options.B: mining is permitted within national parks if a licence is obtained
options.C: the one-kilometre requirement need not apply where a zone had already been prescribed or proposed, while mining within national parks and sanctuaries stays prohibited
options.D: the zone must be ten kilometres in every case

questions.explanation: The passage records the modification and the retained mining prohibition.

questions.question: The Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act, 2023, as described in the passage,

options.A: required benefit-sharing from AYUSH practitioners in every case
options.B: replaced imprisonment for several offences with monetary penalties and exempted AYUSH practitioners and codified traditional knowledge from benefit-sharing
options.C: made every offence under the Act non-bailable
options.D: abolished the National Biodiversity Authority

questions.explanation: The passage records these changes and the criticism that follows.

questions.question: A pharmaceutical company in India wishes to apply for a patent on a drug developed from a plant collected from a forest in India. Under the passage, the company

options.A: needs no approval because it is an Indian entity
options.B: must first obtain the permission of the Central Pollution Control Board
options.C: must apply to the National Green Tribunal for a licence
options.D: needs the prior approval of the National Biodiversity Authority before applying for the intellectual property right

questions.explanation: The passage states the requirement of prior approval for such intellectual property applications.

questions.question: Assertion (A): After the April 2023 modification, mining inside national parks and sanctuaries remains prohibited. Reason (R): The modification relaxed only the blanket one-kilometre requirement and expressly retained the prohibition on mining within national parks and sanctuaries. Which is correct?

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: R states what the modification preserved and so explains A.

passages.title: The Right to Clean Air and the Regulation of the National Capital Region
passages.passage: Article 21 has been read to include the right to a pollution-free environment and the right to clean air, supported by Articles 48A and 51A(g). The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 and the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 form the statutory base, but the severity of air pollution in the National Capital Region led Parliament to enact the Commission for Air Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas Act, 2021. The Act established a statutory Commission with powers to coordinate action, to issue directions to State Governments and industries and to restrict activities affecting air quality; it replaced the Environment Pollution (Prevention and Control) Authority (EPCA) which had been appointed by the Supreme Court. Where a direction of the Commission conflicts with that of a State Government or State Board, the Commission's direction prevails. Contravention is punishable with imprisonment up to five years, or a fine up to Rs 1 crore, or both. The Commission administers the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP), under which progressively stricter measures are triggered by the Air Quality Index: Stage I when air quality is 'Poor' (AQI 201 to 300), Stage II when 'Very Poor' (301 to 400), Stage III when 'Severe' (401 to 450) and Stage IV when 'Severe+' (above 450). In M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (the Taj Trapezium case, 1997), the Court restricted polluting industries around the Taj Mahal, relying on the precautionary principle. In Arjun Gopal v. Union of India, the Court first suspended licences for the sale of firecrackers in Delhi-NCR (2017) and later (2018) permitted only 'green' crackers meeting prescribed emission standards, with restricted hours of use, holding that citizens' right to health outweighed commercial interest. In 2026 the Supreme Court closed the long-running M.C. Mehta proceedings, in which the doctrine of absolute liability and the right to clean air had been developed over four decades; the petitioner said that the fight for clean air must continue.

questions.question: The Commission for Air Quality Management Act, 2021

options.A: established a statutory Commission for the National Capital Region and adjoining areas, replacing the court-appointed EPCA
options.B: abolished the Air Act, 1981
options.C: created a Commission whose directions are subordinate to those of State Governments
options.D: gave the Central Pollution Control Board power to try criminal cases

questions.explanation: The passage describes the Commission as replacing EPCA and prevailing over conflicting State directions.

questions.question: Contravention of a direction of the Commission is punishable with

options.A: imprisonment for life
options.B: imprisonment up to five years, or fine up to Rs 1 crore, or both
options.C: imprisonment up to six months only
options.D: a fine up to Rs 10,000 only

questions.explanation: The passage states the penalty.

questions.question: On a day when the Air Quality Index in Delhi is 430, the applicable stage of GRAP under the passage is

options.A: Stage II
options.B: Stage IV
options.C: Stage III
options.D: Stage I

questions.explanation: An AQI of 401 to 450 falls in the 'Severe' category, which triggers Stage III.

questions.question: A State Government issues a direction on stubble burning which conflicts with a direction of the Commission. Under the passage,

options.A: the matter must be decided by the Supreme Court before either can operate
options.B: the State Government's direction prevails because agriculture is a State subject
options.C: the Commission's direction prevails
options.D: both are void and must be re-issued by the Central Government

questions.explanation: The passage states that the Commission's direction prevails in a conflict.

questions.question: The reasoning of the Supreme Court in Arjun Gopal, as described, was that

options.A: the right to health of citizens outweighed the commercial interest in firecrackers, so that only green crackers were allowed, with restricted hours
options.B: an absolute and permanent ban was constitutionally required
options.C: firecrackers are a fundamental right under Article 19(1)(g) and cannot be regulated
options.D: pollution must be regulated only by the Pollution Control Boards

questions.explanation: The passage records the weighing of health against commerce and the limited permission.

questions.question: Consider the following statements. 1. Contravention of a Commission direction is punishable with imprisonment up to five years, a fine up to Rs 1 crore, or both. 2. EPCA continues to function with priority over the Commission. 3. The Taj Trapezium case relied on the precautionary principle. Which of the statements are correct?

options.A: 1 and 2 only
options.B: 1 and 3 only
options.C: 2 and 3 only
options.D: 1, 2 and 3

questions.explanation: Statements 1 and 3 are correct; EPCA was replaced by the Commission.

passages.title: Workplace Sexual Harassment: From Vishaka to the POSH Act
passages.passage: In Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997), in the absence of legislation, the Supreme Court laid down guidelines to prevent sexual harassment at the workplace, relying on Articles 14, 15, 19(1)(g) and 21 and on the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW), which India ratified in 1993; the guidelines were declared to be the law under Article 141 until legislation was enacted. In Apparel Export Promotion Council v. A.K. Chopra (1999), the Court held that sexual harassment violates the rights to equality and life, and that physical contact is not essential to establish it. Parliament later enacted the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 (POSH Act). The Act defines sexual harassment to include unwelcome physical contact and advances, a demand or request for sexual favours, sexually coloured remarks and showing pornography, and protects any woman, of any age, whether employed or not. 'Workplace' is defined widely and includes a dwelling place or house. Every employer with ten or more employees must constitute an Internal Committee (IC) at each office or branch, presided over by a senior woman employee, with at least half of its members women and one external member from an NGO or association committed to the cause of women. Where an establishment has fewer than ten employees, or where the complaint is against the employer, the complaint goes to the Local Committee at the district level. A complaint must be made within three months of the incident, extendable by a further three months for reasons recorded. The Committee may, at the request of the aggrieved woman, take steps for conciliation before the inquiry begins, but monetary settlement cannot be the basis of conciliation. The inquiry is to be completed within ninety days. An employer who fails to constitute the Committee is liable to a fine up to Rs 50,000, doubled for repetition, and may face cancellation of licence. In Aureliano Fernandes v. State of Goa (2023), the Supreme Court found widespread non-compliance and issued time-bound directions for the constitution of Committees in all bodies.

questions.question: The Vishaka guidelines were issued by the Supreme Court on the basis of

options.A: Article 32 alone, without reference to any right
options.B: Articles 14, 15, 19(1)(g) and 21 read with CEDAW, as the law declared until legislation was enacted
options.C: an international court's direction to India
options.D: a statute passed by Parliament in 1993

questions.explanation: The passage records the constitutional provisions, CEDAW and the declaration under Article 141.

questions.question: An Internal Committee must be constituted by an employer who has

options.A: more than fifty employees
options.B: at least one woman employee
options.C: ten or more employees at an office or branch
options.D: any number of employees, but only on a complaint

questions.explanation: The passage states the threshold of ten employees.

questions.question: A complaint of sexual harassment under the POSH Act must ordinarily be made within

options.A: one year of the incident, without extension
options.B: thirty days, without extension
options.C: six months, extendable by one year
options.D: three months of the incident, extendable by a further three months for reasons recorded

questions.explanation: The passage states the limitation and extension.

questions.question: On conciliation under the POSH Act, the passage indicates that

options.A: it can be initiated by the employer against the wishes of the woman
options.B: it may be attempted at the request of the aggrieved woman before inquiry, but monetary settlement cannot be its basis
options.C: it must be attempted in every case before a complaint is accepted
options.D: it may be based on payment of money by the respondent

questions.explanation: The passage states both the timing and the bar on monetary settlement.

questions.question: A domestic worker alleges that her employer sexually harassed her in his home, where there are no other employees. Her complaint should go to

options.A: the Pollution Control Board
options.B: the Local Committee at the district level
options.C: the Supreme Court under Article 32 alone
options.D: the Internal Committee of the employer's household

questions.explanation: A dwelling place is a workplace, and a complaint against the employer or from a small establishment goes to the Local Committee.

questions.question: The consequence for an employer who fails to constitute the Internal Committee is

options.A: imprisonment for one year in every case
options.B: a fine of Rs 10 crore
options.C: no penalty, since the Act is only directory
options.D: a fine up to Rs 50,000, doubled for repetition, with possible cancellation of licence

questions.explanation: The passage states the penalty.

passages.title: Women at Work: Maternity Protection and Equal Pay
passages.passage: Article 15(3) permits special provisions for women, Article 39(d) directs the State to secure equal pay for equal work for men and women, and Article 42 requires just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief. In Air India v. Nargesh Meerza (1981), the Supreme Court struck down a regulation terminating an air hostess on her first pregnancy as arbitrary and contrary to the notions of a civilised society. In Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Female Workers (Muster Roll) (2000), the Court held that maternity benefit extends to casual and daily-wage women workers. The Maternity Benefit Act, 1961, as amended in 2017, gave 26 weeks of paid leave for the first two children and 12 weeks where the woman already had two surviving children; adoptive and commissioning mothers received 12 weeks; and establishments with fifty or more employees had to provide a crèche. The Code on Social Security, 2020, which came into force on 21 November 2025 and consolidated these provisions, carries the scheme forward. In K. Umadevi v. Government of Tamil Nadu (May 2025), the Supreme Court held that maternity benefits are part of reproductive rights and that maternity leave is integral to them, so that a State rule could not defeat the statutory entitlement of a government teacher who had two children from an earlier marriage and sought leave for her first child from her second marriage; the Court held that there is no cap on the number of children for claiming the benefit, though its duration is shorter where the woman has two or more surviving children. In Hamsaanandini Nanduri v. Union of India (17 March 2026), the Court struck down Section 60(4) of the Code, which limited the benefit for adoptive mothers to cases where the child was below three months, holding that the classification violated Articles 14 and 21, and it urged the Union to recognise paternity leave as a social security benefit. On wages, the Code on Wages, 2019 prohibits discrimination on the ground of gender in wages for the same work or work of a similar nature, and subsumes the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976.

questions.question: Under the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961, as amended in 2017 and described in the passage, a woman with fewer than two surviving children is entitled to paid maternity leave of

options.A: 12 weeks
options.B: 26 weeks
options.C: six months and one day
options.D: 16 weeks

questions.explanation: The passage gives 26 weeks for the first two children.

questions.question: In the Female Workers (Muster Roll) case, the Supreme Court held that maternity benefit

options.A: applies only to women employed in factories
options.B: is a concession which the employer may withdraw
options.C: is limited to permanent employees
options.D: extends to casual and daily-wage women workers

questions.explanation: The passage records this extension.

questions.question: The regulation struck down in Nargesh Meerza was one that

options.A: permitted equal pay for all cabin crew
options.B: required air hostesses to retire at sixty
options.C: fixed a minimum height for air hostesses
options.D: terminated an air hostess on her first pregnancy

questions.explanation: The Court found the termination rule arbitrary.

questions.question: A State Government employee already has two surviving children from an earlier marriage. She bears a child in her second marriage and seeks maternity leave, which the State refuses on the ground that it would be her third child. In the light of the passage,

options.A: she is entitled to maternity benefit, although its duration is shorter as she has two surviving children
options.B: she is entitled only to adoption leave
options.C: she is entitled to 26 weeks as for a first child
options.D: she has no claim because the State rule prevails over the statute

questions.explanation: Umadevi holds that there is no cap on children for claiming the benefit, with shorter duration where two or more children survive.

questions.question: A woman adopts a child aged eight months and is refused maternity benefit under Section 60(4) of the Code on Social Security, 2020, which limits it to children below three months. Following the 2026 decision, the refusal is

options.A: unsustainable, since the age limit was struck down as violating Articles 14 and 21
options.B: valid only if the employer has fewer than fifty employees
options.C: valid, since adoption does not create reproductive rights
options.D: valid, since the Code is a later Act

questions.explanation: Hamsaanandini Nanduri struck down the three-month limit.

questions.question: Assertion (A): The Code on Wages, 2019 gives statutory form to the constitutional goal of equal pay for equal work. Reason (R): Article 39(d) directs the State to secure equal pay for equal work for men and women, and the Code prohibits wage discrimination on the ground of gender. Which is correct?

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: R states the constitutional directive and the statutory prohibition which together support A.

passages.title: Reproductive Autonomy and the Medical Termination of Pregnancy
passages.passage: Reproductive autonomy has been recognised as part of personal liberty under Article 21. In Suchita Srivastava v. Chandigarh Administration (2009), the Supreme Court held that a woman's right to make reproductive choices is a dimension of personal liberty, and that her consent is paramount even where she has an intellectual disability. In K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), the Court recognised decisional autonomy, including choices on reproduction, as part of privacy. The Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act, 1971, as amended in 2021, permits termination up to twenty weeks on the opinion of one registered medical practitioner, and between twenty and twenty-four weeks, on the opinion of two practitioners, for specified categories of women: survivors of rape or sexual assault, minors, women whose marital status has changed during the pregnancy, women with physical disabilities or mental illness, and women in humanitarian or disaster settings. There is no upper limit where a Medical Board diagnoses substantial foetal abnormalities. The amended Act speaks of 'woman' and 'partner' in place of 'married woman' and 'husband', so as to include unmarried women who face contraceptive failure. In X v. Principal Secretary, Health and Family Welfare Department, Government of NCT of Delhi (2022), the Court held that unmarried women between twenty and twenty-four weeks are entitled to the same access as married women, since the distinction was artificial and unconstitutional, and that, for the purposes of the Rules, marital rape counts as sexual assault. The Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (Prohibition of Sex Selection) Act, 1994 bans sex determination in order to address the declining sex ratio; in Voluntary Health Association of Punjab v. Union of India (2013), the Court directed its strict implementation. The Surrogacy (Regulation) Act, 2021 permits only altruistic surrogacy and prohibits commercial surrogacy. In K. Umadevi (2025), the Court observed that reproductive rights include the rights to health, privacy, dignity and equality.

questions.question: In Suchita Srivastava, the Supreme Court held that reproductive choice is

options.A: a right available only to married women
options.B: subject to the consent of the husband in all cases
options.C: a Directive Principle only
options.D: a dimension of personal liberty under Article 21, in which the woman's consent is paramount

questions.explanation: The passage records this holding.

questions.question: Termination between twenty and twenty-four weeks, on the opinion of two practitioners, is available under the 2021 Act to

options.A: married women only
options.B: specified categories such as survivors of sexual assault and minors
options.C: women whose pregnancy has been confirmed by a Medical Board only
options.D: any woman, for any reason

questions.explanation: The passage lists the specified categories.

questions.question: In X v. Principal Secretary (2022), the Supreme Court held that

options.A: termination after twenty weeks requires the husband's consent
options.B: only married women may seek termination after twenty weeks
options.C: unmarried women between twenty and twenty-four weeks are entitled to the same access as married women
options.D: unmarried women must first obtain a court order

questions.explanation: The distinction between married and unmarried women was held artificial and unconstitutional.

questions.question: A woman in the twenty-seventh week of pregnancy is found by a Medical Board to be carrying a foetus with substantial abnormalities. On the passage,

options.A: termination requires the husband's consent
options.B: termination is barred in every case after twenty-four weeks
options.C: termination may be permitted, since there is no upper limit where a Medical Board diagnoses substantial foetal abnormalities
options.D: termination requires the opinion of one practitioner only

questions.explanation: The 2021 Act removes the time limit for substantial foetal abnormalities diagnosed by a Medical Board.

questions.question: Consider the following statements. 1. The amended Act uses the words 'woman' and 'partner' in place of 'married woman' and 'husband'. 2. Termination up to twenty weeks always requires the opinion of two practitioners. 3. In X v. Principal Secretary, the Court held that, for the purposes of the Rules, marital rape counts as sexual assault. Which of the statements are correct?

options.A: 1 and 2 only
options.B: 1 and 3 only
options.C: 2 and 3 only
options.D: 1, 2 and 3

questions.explanation: Statements 1 and 3 are correct; up to twenty weeks one practitioner's opinion suffices.

questions.question: Assertion (A): Access to termination of pregnancy under the amended Act is not confined to married women. Reason (R): The amended Act substitutes 'woman' and 'partner' for 'married woman' and 'husband'. Which is correct?

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: The change of wording is the textual basis for the inclusion of unmarried women.

passages.title: Women's Political Representation: Panchayats to Parliament
passages.passage: The 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992) require that one-third of the seats in Panchayats and Municipalities, and of the offices of chairpersons, be reserved for women, including women of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Articles 243D and 243T). No corresponding reservation existed for Parliament or State Legislatures until the Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, 2023, the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, which inserted Articles 330A and 332A to reserve one-third of the seats in the House of the People and the State Legislative Assemblies for women, including one-third of the seats reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, and extended the same to the Legislative Assembly of Delhi. The reservation does not extend to the Rajya Sabha or State Legislative Councils. Under Article 334A, the reservation is to take effect only after a delimitation exercise undertaken following the first census taken after the commencement of the Act, is to continue for fifteen years, and the reserved seats are to be rotated after each delimitation. The Act was brought into force by a notification effective 16 April 2026, but because delimitation must follow the next census, due in 2027, the reservation did not apply to the 2024 general election and, after the failure of a fast-track package, is widely expected not to apply in 2029. In April 2026 the Union introduced three Bills, including the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, to base delimitation on the 2011 census so that the reservation could operate by 2029; the package did not secure Parliament's approval. A Bill to amend the Constitution must, under Article 368(2), be passed by a majority of the total membership of each House and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting. Supporters regard the reservation as essential to substantive equality, while critics have objected to the delay and to the absence of a sub-quota for Other Backward Class women.

questions.question: Article 243D, inserted by the 73rd Amendment, requires reservation for women of

options.A: one-fourth of the seats in Municipalities only
options.B: one-third of the seats in Panchayats, including seats reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes
options.C: one-third of the seats in the Rajya Sabha
options.D: one-half of the seats in the Lok Sabha

questions.explanation: The passage states the Panchayat reservation.

questions.question: The reservation under the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam does NOT extend to

options.A: State Legislative Assemblies
options.B: the Legislative Assembly of Delhi
options.C: the Rajya Sabha and State Legislative Councils
options.D: the House of the People

questions.explanation: The passage states the exclusion of the Rajya Sabha and Legislative Councils.

questions.question: The notification bringing the Act into force with effect from 16 April 2026

options.A: repealed Article 334A
options.B: brought the Act into force, but reserved seats become operative only after delimitation following the next census
options.C: extended the reservation to the Rajya Sabha
options.D: reserved one-third of the seats in the Lok Sabha with immediate effect

questions.explanation: Article 334A makes operation depend on delimitation after the first census after commencement.

questions.question: Within the seats reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, the 2023 Act provides that

options.A: all seats shall be reserved for women
options.B: one-half shall be reserved for women
options.C: no seats shall be reserved for women
options.D: one-third shall be reserved for women belonging to those categories

questions.explanation: The passage states the one-third rule within SC and ST seats.

questions.question: For the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill to be passed, Article 368(2) requires

options.A: a majority of the total membership of each House and a two-thirds majority of members present and voting
options.B: approval of the President alone
options.C: a unanimous vote of both Houses
options.D: a simple majority of members present and voting

questions.explanation: The passage states the special majority under Article 368(2).

questions.question: Assertion (A): The 2023 Act gave women no reserved seats at the 2024 general election. Reason (R): Article 334A makes the reservation operative only after delimitation following the first census taken after the Act's commencement. Which is correct?

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: R states the condition which postponed operation of the reservation.

passages.title: Domestic Violence, Cruelty and Dowry Death
passages.passage: The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 (PWDVA) gives civil remedies to women in a domestic relationship, which includes marriage and relationships in the nature of marriage. A Magistrate may grant protection orders, residence orders, monetary relief, custody orders and compensation. A woman has a right to reside in the 'shared household' whether or not she has any title in it. In S.R. Batra v. Taruna Batra (2006), the Supreme Court held that a house owned exclusively by the husband's mother was not a shared household; in Satish Chander Ahuja v. Sneha Ahuja (2020), a three-judge Bench overruled that view, holding that a shared household is not confined to premises owned or rented by the husband and includes the household in which the woman has lived in a domestic relationship. In Hiral P. Harsora v. Kusum Narottamdas Harsora (2016), the Court struck down the words 'adult male' in the definition of respondent, so that a complaint may be made against female relatives as well. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 deals with criminal liability. Section 85 punishes cruelty by a husband or his relatives with imprisonment up to three years and fine. Section 86 defines cruelty as wilful conduct likely to drive a woman to suicide or cause grave injury to her life, limb or health, and harassment of her with a view to coercing her or her relatives to meet an unlawful demand for property. Section 80 deals with dowry death: where a woman dies otherwise than in normal circumstances within seven years of marriage, and it is shown that soon before her death she was subjected to cruelty or harassment by her husband or his relatives in connection with a demand for dowry, they are deemed to have caused the death, punishable with imprisonment of not less than seven years which may extend to life; the law of evidence raises a presumption in such cases. In Dara Lakshmi Narayana v. State of Telangana (2024), the Supreme Court cautioned against the misuse of the cruelty provision through general and omnibus allegations against relatives. In Satender Kumar Antil v. CBI (2026), the Court reiterated that, for offences punishable up to seven years, a notice under Section 35(3) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 is the rule and arrest the exception.

questions.question: Section 85 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 punishes cruelty by a husband or his relatives with

options.A: a fine only
options.B: imprisonment up to three years and fine
options.C: imprisonment for life
options.D: imprisonment up to ten years and fine

questions.explanation: The passage states the punishment.

questions.question: In Satish Chander Ahuja v. Sneha Ahuja, the Supreme Court held that a 'shared household'

options.A: means only a house in which the wife holds legal title
options.B: excludes any house owned by the husband's parents
options.C: is not confined to premises owned or rented by the husband and includes the household in which the woman has lived in a domestic relationship
options.D: means only a house owned by the husband

questions.explanation: The three-judge Bench overruled the narrower view in S.R. Batra.

questions.question: The effect of the decision in Hiral Harsora was that

options.A: complaints may be made only against the husband
options.B: the Act was held unconstitutional
options.C: a complaint under the PWDVA may be made against female relatives as well, since the words 'adult male' were struck down
options.D: residence orders may no longer be granted

questions.explanation: The passage records the striking down of the words 'adult male'.

questions.question: A married woman is found hanging at her husband's house nine years after her marriage, and evidence shows that she was harassed for dowry until shortly before her death. On the passage, the offence of dowry death under Section 80 is

options.A: attracted only if the husband confesses
options.B: not attracted, since the death did not occur within seven years of marriage
options.C: attracted, since harassment for dowry is shown
options.D: attracted, since the woman died at her husband's house

questions.explanation: Section 80 requires death within seven years of marriage; other provisions may still apply.

questions.question: The caution administered by the Supreme Court in Dara Lakshmi Narayana concerned

options.A: the abolition of the cruelty provision
options.B: the need to arrest the accused at once in every case
options.C: the exclusion of relatives from all liability
options.D: the misuse of the cruelty provision through general and omnibus allegations against relatives

questions.explanation: The passage records this caution.

questions.question: Which of the following conduct falls within 'cruelty' as defined in Section 86, as described in the passage?

options.A: The husband's absence from home for work
options.B: Harassment of a woman to coerce her or her relatives into meeting an unlawful demand for property
options.C: A single ordinary domestic quarrel without harassment or danger
options.D: A difference of religious opinion between spouses

questions.explanation: The definition includes harassment to coerce an unlawful demand for property.

passages.title: Offences Against Women under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita
passages.passage: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 groups offences against women in a dedicated chapter. Section 63 defines rape, and Section 64 prescribes rigorous imprisonment of not less than ten years, which may extend to life. Section 70 deals with gang rape, punishable with rigorous imprisonment of not less than twenty years which may extend to life, while gang rape of a woman under eighteen is punishable with imprisonment for life, meaning the remainder of natural life, or with death. Section 72 prohibits disclosure of the identity of a victim of certain offences, and Section 73 prohibits printing or publishing court proceedings relating to such an offence without the court's permission; each is punishable with imprisonment up to two years and fine. Section 74 penalises assault or criminal force to a woman with intent to outrage her modesty with imprisonment of not less than one year, which may extend to five years, and fine. Section 75 deals with sexual harassment: unwelcome physical contact and advances, a demand or request for sexual favours, or showing pornography against her will is punishable with imprisonment up to three years, fine, or both, while making sexually coloured remarks is punishable with imprisonment up to one year, fine, or both. Section 76 punishes assault or use of criminal force with intent to disrobe a woman with imprisonment of not less than three years, extendable to seven, and fine. Section 77 makes voyeurism an offence, punishable on first conviction with imprisonment of one to three years and on a subsequent conviction with three to seven years. Section 78 punishes stalking with imprisonment up to three years on first conviction and up to five years on a subsequent conviction, with fine. Section 79 punishes the use of a word, gesture or act intended to insult the modesty of a woman with imprisonment up to three years and fine. Section 124 deals with acid attacks: voluntarily causing grievous hurt by acid is punishable with imprisonment of not less than ten years which may extend to life, with a fine that must be just and reasonable to meet the victim's medical expenses, while throwing or attempting to throw acid is punishable with five to seven years and fine.

questions.question: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt by the use of acid is punishable under Section 124 with imprisonment of

options.A: not less than ten years, which may extend to life, and fine
options.B: up to five years only
options.C: not less than five years, extending to seven years
options.D: not less than one year, extending to three years

questions.explanation: The passage states the punishment for grievous hurt by acid; five to seven years is for throwing or attempting to throw acid.

questions.question: A man who has already been convicted of stalking is convicted of stalking a second time. The maximum imprisonment under Section 78 is

options.A: five years
options.B: ten years
options.C: three years
options.D: seven years

questions.explanation: The passage gives up to five years on a subsequent conviction.

questions.question: A colleague repeatedly makes sexually coloured remarks to a woman but does not touch her, demand favours or show her pornography. The maximum imprisonment under Section 75 for such conduct is

options.A: three years
options.B: seven years
options.C: one year
options.D: five years

questions.explanation: Sexually coloured remarks attract imprisonment up to one year; the other forms attract up to three years.

questions.question: On a first conviction for voyeurism under Section 77, the punishment is imprisonment for

options.A: not less than ten years
options.B: one to three years, with fine
options.C: up to one year only
options.D: three to seven years, with fine

questions.explanation: The passage gives one to three years for a first conviction and three to seven for a subsequent one.

questions.question: A newspaper prints the name of a victim of rape in its report without any court permission. On the passage, the editor-in-charge is liable under

options.A: Section 124, with imprisonment up to life
options.B: Section 64, with imprisonment of not less than ten years
options.C: Section 72, with imprisonment up to two years and fine
options.D: Section 78, with imprisonment up to three years

questions.explanation: Section 72 penalises disclosure of the victim's identity.

questions.question: Consider the following statements. 1. Section 74 prescribes imprisonment of not less than one year for assault or criminal force with intent to outrage a woman's modesty. 2. Section 76 prescribes imprisonment of not less than three years, extendable to seven, for assault or criminal force with intent to disrobe a woman. 3. Section 79 prescribes imprisonment for life for a word or gesture intended to insult the modesty of a woman. Which of the statements are correct?

options.A: 1 and 2 only
options.B: 1 and 3 only
options.C: 2 and 3 only
options.D: 1, 2 and 3

questions.explanation: Statements 1 and 2 are correct; Section 79 carries imprisonment up to three years.

passages.title: Homicide, Negligence and Abetment of Suicide under the BNS
