passages.passage: Section 100 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 defines culpable homicide, and Section 101 defines murder, which is culpable homicide if the act is done with the intention of causing death, or with the intention of causing bodily injury which the offender knows is likely to cause death, or with the intention of causing bodily injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, or with knowledge that the act is so imminently dangerous that it must in all probability cause death. Exceptions reduce murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder, as in the case of grave and sudden provocation, exceeding in good faith the right of private defence, or a sudden fight in the heat of passion. In Virsa Singh v. State of Punjab (1958), the Supreme Court held that, for the third limb, the prosecution must establish that a bodily injury was present, what its nature was, that it was intentionally inflicted, and that it was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death; the intention required is to inflict that particular injury, and not merely to strike. Section 103(1) punishes murder with death or imprisonment for life and fine, and Section 103(2) provides the same punishment where a group of five or more persons acting in concert commits murder on the ground of race, caste, community, sex, place of birth, language or personal belief. Section 104 provides that a person undergoing a sentence of imprisonment for life who commits murder shall be punished with death or with imprisonment for life, which means the remainder of his natural life. Section 105 punishes culpable homicide not amounting to murder with imprisonment for life, or for five to ten years, and fine, where the act was done with the intention of causing death or injury likely to cause death, and with imprisonment up to ten years, and fine, where it was done only with knowledge. Section 106(1) punishes death caused by a rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide with imprisonment up to five years and fine, reduced to two years where the act is that of a registered medical practitioner during a medical procedure. Section 106(2) provides for imprisonment up to ten years and fine where death is caused by rash and negligent driving and the driver escapes without reporting it to a police officer or Magistrate soon after; the provision attracted protests from transporters. Section 108 punishes abetment of suicide with imprisonment up to ten years and fine.

questions.question: A person undergoing a sentence of imprisonment for life commits murder. Under Section 104, he is punishable with

options.A: imprisonment for not less than five years
options.B: imprisonment for ten years only
options.C: death or imprisonment for life, which means the remainder of his natural life
options.D: a fine only

questions.explanation: The passage states Section 104.

questions.question: A registered medical practitioner causes the death of a patient by a rash act during a medical procedure, not amounting to culpable homicide. The maximum imprisonment under Section 106(1) is

options.A: ten years
options.B: five years
options.C: seven years
options.D: two years

questions.explanation: The passage states that the term is reduced to two years for such practitioners.

questions.question: A driver causes death by rash and negligent driving and flees without reporting the accident to the police or a Magistrate. The maximum imprisonment under Section 106(2) is

options.A: ten years, with fine
options.B: life imprisonment
options.C: two years, with fine
options.D: five years, with fine

questions.explanation: The passage states ten years and fine.

questions.question: Which of the following need NOT be proved to establish murder under the third limb of Section 101, according to Virsa Singh?

options.A: That the injury was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death
options.B: That the injury was intentionally inflicted
options.C: That a bodily injury was present
options.D: An intention to cause the death of the victim

questions.explanation: For the third limb the intention required is to inflict the particular injury, not to cause death.

questions.question: A strikes B a single blow on the head with an iron rod, intending to inflict that blow. The injury is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, and B dies. A says he did not intend to kill. On the passage, A is most likely guilty of

options.A: simple hurt only
options.B: death by negligence under Section 106(1)
options.C: culpable homicide not amounting to murder on the ground of absence of intention to kill
options.D: murder under the third limb of Section 101

questions.explanation: Virsa Singh requires intention to inflict the injury, not intention to kill.

questions.question: Consider the following statements. 1. Section 106(1) provides imprisonment up to five years for all persons, including medical practitioners, without distinction. 2. Section 103(2) applies where a group of five or more persons acting in concert commits murder on certain prohibited grounds. 3. Section 108 punishes abetment of suicide with imprisonment up to ten years and fine. Which of the statements are correct?

options.A: 1 and 2 only
options.B: 1 and 3 only
options.C: 2 and 3 only
options.D: 1, 2 and 3

questions.explanation: Statements 2 and 3 are correct; medical practitioners are subject to a lower maximum of two years.

passages.title: Arrest, Investigation and Trial Timelines under the BNSS
passages.passage: Section 35 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) governs arrest without warrant. For an offence punishable with imprisonment up to seven years, the police may arrest only if satisfied that arrest is necessary, for example to prevent further offence, to ensure proper investigation, to prevent tampering with evidence or the inducement of witnesses, or to secure the accused's presence in court, and must record reasons; otherwise a notice of appearance under Section 35(3) must be issued, and if the person complies he is not to be arrested unless reasons are recorded. In Satender Kumar Antil v. Central Bureau of Investigation (2026), the Supreme Court held that, for such offences, notice is the rule and arrest the exception, and that where the person fails to comply, arrest under Section 35(6) is not automatic and must rest on fresh material not available when the notice was issued. For offences punishable with three years or more but less than seven, Section 173(3) allows the officer, with the prior permission of an officer not below the rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police, to hold a preliminary enquiry within fourteen days to determine whether a prima facie case exists. Section 176(3) requires a forensic expert to visit the scene and collect evidence in offences punishable with imprisonment of seven years or more. The police must inform the informant or victim of the progress of the investigation within ninety days (Section 193). Section 479 provides that an undertrial who has been detained for one-third of the maximum sentence, if a first-time offender, or for one-half in other cases, shall be released on bail; it does not apply to offences punishable with death or life imprisonment, and in 2024 the Supreme Court directed that it applies to all undertrials irrespective of when their cases were registered. Under Section 392, a judgment is to be pronounced within forty-five days of the conclusion of arguments, and Section 230 requires the supply of the police report and documents to the accused within fourteen days of the accused's appearance.

questions.question: For an offence punishable with imprisonment up to seven years, the BNSS requires that the police ordinarily

options.A: obtain a warrant from the High Court before arrest
options.B: arrest the accused at once and issue notice afterwards
options.C: register the case only after a preliminary enquiry of ninety days
options.D: issue a notice of appearance under Section 35(3), arrest being the exception

questions.explanation: The passage states that notice is the rule.

questions.question: According to Satender Kumar Antil (2026), where an accused has failed to comply with a notice under Section 35(3), arrest under Section 35(6)

options.A: may be made only with the permission of the Supreme Court
options.B: is barred in every case
options.C: is automatic and requires no reasons
options.D: is not automatic and must rest on fresh material not available when the notice was issued

questions.explanation: The passage states this holding.

questions.question: A preliminary enquiry under Section 173(3) BNSS may be held

options.A: only in offences punishable with death
options.B: only by a Magistrate
options.C: in offences punishable with three years or more but less than seven, within fourteen days, with the prior permission of an officer not below Deputy Superintendent of Police
options.D: in every offence, without permission, within ninety days

questions.explanation: The passage states the conditions.

questions.question: Under Section 193 of the BNSS, the police must inform the informant or victim of the progress of investigation within

options.A: ninety days
options.B: one year
options.C: fourteen days
options.D: forty-five days

questions.explanation: The passage states ninety days.

questions.question: A first-time offender, accused of an offence punishable with a maximum of six years, has been in custody as an undertrial for two and a half years. On the passage, he is

options.A: not entitled, as he must first serve one-half of the maximum sentence
options.B: entitled only if the trial court consents in writing
options.C: entitled to be released on bail, since he has been detained for more than one-third of the maximum sentence
options.D: not entitled, because Section 479 applies only to offences punishable with life imprisonment

questions.explanation: One-third of six years is two years; he has been detained longer.

questions.question: Consider the following statements. 1. Section 173(3) allows a preliminary enquiry within fourteen days in specified offences, with the prior permission of an officer not below the rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police. 2. Section 479 applies to offences punishable with life imprisonment. 3. A judgment is to be pronounced within forty-five days of the conclusion of arguments. Which of the statements are correct?

options.A: 1 and 2 only
options.B: 1 and 3 only
options.C: 2 and 3 only
options.D: 1, 2 and 3

questions.explanation: Statements 1 and 3 are correct; Section 479 does not apply to offences punishable with death or life imprisonment.

passages.title: Digital Evidence, Search and Seizure under the BNSS and the BSA
passages.passage: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) bring electronic processes into criminal justice. Under Section 105 of the BNSS, the process of search and seizure, including the preparation of the list of seized items, must be recorded through audio-video electronic means, preferably by mobile phone, and the recording forwarded forthwith to the District Magistrate, Sub-Divisional Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate of the first class. Section 94 empowers a court or police officer to summon the production of any document or other thing, and 'document' includes electronic and digital records. Section 107 provides that a court may order the attachment or forfeiture of property which is the proceeds of crime, on an application by a police officer approved by a Superintendent of Police. Section 349 allows a Magistrate to order any person, whether or not arrested, to give specimen signatures, handwriting, finger impressions or voice samples. Section 530 permits trials and other proceedings to be held in electronic mode. Under the BSA, 'document' includes electronic or digital records, and an electronic record is not inadmissible only because it is electronic. Section 63 sets out the conditions of admissibility of an electronic record and requires a certificate in the prescribed Schedule, in two parts: Part A signed by the person in charge of the device or by the party, and Part B signed by an expert, together with the hash value of the record. In Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer (2014), the Supreme Court held that secondary electronic evidence requires such a certificate. In Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v. Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal (2020), a three-judge Bench held that the certificate is a condition precedent to admissibility where the original is not produced, overruling Shafhi Mohammad, but that it may be produced at any stage before the trial concludes, and that the court may direct its production in appropriate cases.

questions.question: Under Section 105 of the BNSS, the process of search and seizure must be

options.A: recorded only in writing by the investigating officer
options.B: witnessed only by the informant
options.C: recorded through audio-video electronic means, preferably by mobile phone, and forwarded forthwith to a Magistrate
options.D: carried out only with a warrant of the High Court

questions.explanation: The passage states the recording requirement.

questions.question: The certificate under Section 63 of the BSA is to be given in

options.A: a single part signed by the investigating officer
options.B: two parts, both signed by the Magistrate
options.C: a single part signed by the accused
options.D: two parts, Part A signed by the person in charge of the device or the party, and Part B signed by an expert

questions.explanation: The passage describes the two-part certificate.

questions.question: Arjun Panditrao Khotkar held that the certificate for electronic evidence

options.A: is required only for documents stored in paper form
options.B: is never required for electronic evidence
options.C: is a condition precedent where the original is not produced, but may be produced at any stage before the trial concludes
options.D: must be produced before the charge-sheet is filed

questions.explanation: The passage records this holding and the overruling of Shafhi Mohammad.

questions.question: Under Section 107 of the BNSS, attachment or forfeiture of property which is the proceeds of crime may be ordered by

options.A: the Superintendent of Police, without a court order
options.B: a court, on the application of a police officer approved by a Superintendent of Police
options.C: the investigating officer alone, without any approval
options.D: the accused with the consent of the victim

questions.explanation: The passage states the procedure.

questions.question: The police produce at trial a copy of CCTV footage stored on a pen drive, without the Section 63 certificate. Before the trial concludes, the prosecution offers a certificate. In the light of Arjun Panditrao, the court

options.A: must treat the footage as primary evidence without any certificate in every case
options.B: may permit the certificate to be produced, as it may be produced at any stage before the trial concludes
options.C: must reject the footage, as electronic evidence is inadmissible
options.D: must reject the footage, since the certificate had to be filed with the charge-sheet

questions.explanation: The Court allowed production at any stage before the conclusion of the trial.

questions.question: Under Section 349 of the BNSS, a Magistrate may order a person to give voice samples

options.A: only if the person has been arrested
options.B: only with the consent of the High Court
options.C: whether or not that person has been arrested
options.D: only after the person has been convicted

questions.explanation: The passage states that the power extends to persons not arrested.

passages.title: Common Intention, Common Object, Conspiracy and Abetment under the BNS
passages.passage: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 contains several provisions on liability for acts done by more than one person. Section 3(5) provides that, when a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance of the common intention of all, each is liable as if the act were done by him alone. The provision does not create a substantive offence but states a rule of joint liability; it requires a prior meeting of minds, which may develop on the spot, and, according to Barendra Kumar Ghosh v. King Emperor (1925), a person who merely stands and waits at a place in furtherance of the plan may also be liable. Section 190 deals with common object: where an offence is committed by any member of an unlawful assembly, that is, an assembly of five or more persons with a common unlawful object, in prosecution of that object, or of a kind which the members knew was likely to be committed, every member is guilty of the offence. Active participation is not required; it suffices that the accused was a member of the assembly. Section 61 defines criminal conspiracy as an agreement between two or more persons to do or cause to be done an illegal act, or a legal act by illegal means; an agreement to commit an offence is punishable without more, but an agreement to do any other illegal act requires some act besides the agreement. In Kehar Singh v. State (Delhi Administration) (1988), the Supreme Court observed that direct proof of conspiracy is rarely available and that the agreement may be inferred from circumstances. Abetment under Section 45 may be by instigation, by conspiracy with an act or illegal omission in pursuance of it, or by intentional aid. Under Section 54, an abettor who is present when the offence is committed is deemed to have committed it.

questions.question: Under Section 3(5) of the BNS, where a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance of the common intention of all,

options.A: only the person who actually commits the act is liable
options.B: each is liable for the act as if it were done by him alone
options.C: all are liable only for abetment
options.D: liability arises only if five or more persons are involved

questions.explanation: The passage states the rule of joint liability.

questions.question: The principal difference between Section 190 (common object) and Section 3(5) (common intention) is that Section 190 requires

options.A: membership of an unlawful assembly of five or more persons, and not active participation in the act
options.B: a prior meeting of minds among exactly two persons
options.C: an agreement to commit an offence, and not any assembly
options.D: proof that every accused personally struck the victim

questions.explanation: The passage states that membership of the assembly suffices under Section 190.

questions.question: According to Barendra Kumar Ghosh, a person who stands guard outside a house while his companions commit an offence within, in furtherance of their plan, is

options.A: liable, as one who merely stands and waits in furtherance of the plan may also be liable
options.B: liable only for abetment
options.C: not liable, since he did not take part in the act
options.D: liable only if he carries a weapon

questions.explanation: The passage records the principle of the case.

questions.question: Under Section 61, a criminal conspiracy to do an illegal act which is not an offence is complete only when

options.A: a Magistrate has recorded the agreement
options.B: some act besides the agreement is done by one or more of the parties
options.C: five or more persons have joined it
options.D: the parties merely meet and agree

questions.explanation: The passage states that an overt act is required for such conspiracies.

questions.question: Six persons assemble with the common object of beating X. One of them, unknown to the others, brings a gun and shoots X dead. On the passage, the liability of the other five for murder depends on

options.A: whether they were present when the gun was bought
options.B: whether the assembly was lawful
options.C: whether they knew that murder was likely to be committed in prosecution of the common object
options.D: whether any of them fired at X

questions.explanation: Section 190 extends liability to offences the members knew were likely to be committed.

questions.question: Consider the following statements. 1. Section 3(5) does not create a substantive offence but states a rule of joint liability. 2. A person can be held liable under Section 190 only if he actively participated in the offence. 3. An abettor who is present when the offence is committed is deemed to have committed it. Which of the statements are correct?

options.A: 1 and 2 only
options.B: 1 and 3 only
options.C: 2 and 3 only
options.D: 1, 2 and 3

questions.explanation: Statements 1 and 3 are correct; Section 190 does not require active participation.

passages.title: Corporate Social Responsibility, ESG and the Stakeholder Company
passages.passage: Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013 and the CSR Rules require companies with a net worth of Rs 500 crore or more, turnover of Rs 1,000 crore or more, or net profit of Rs 5 crore or more in the immediately preceding financial year to constitute a Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) Committee and to spend at least two per cent of the average net profits of the preceding three financial years on activities listed in Schedule VII, which include eradicating hunger and poverty, promoting education, promoting gender equality and empowering women, ensuring environmental sustainability and protecting national heritage. Where the unspent amount relates to an ongoing project, it must be transferred to an Unspent CSR Account within thirty days of the end of the financial year and spent within three years; otherwise it must be transferred to a fund specified in Schedule VII within six months. Following the 2019 amendment, a company in default is liable to a penalty of twice the unspent amount or Rs 1 crore, whichever is less, and each officer in default to one-tenth of the unspent amount or Rs 2 lakh, whichever is less. Section 166(2) requires a director to act in good faith to promote the objects of the company for the benefit of its members as a whole and in the best interests of the company, its employees, the shareholders, the community and for the protection of the environment. Section 149(1) requires prescribed classes of companies, including listed companies and public companies with paid-up share capital of Rs 100 crore or more or turnover of Rs 300 crore or more, to have at least one woman director. The Securities and Exchange Board of India requires the top one thousand listed companies by market capitalisation to file a Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR) disclosing their environmental, social and governance performance, with assurance of core indicators phased in beginning with the top 150. These provisions reflect a shift from a shareholder-centred view of the company towards a stakeholder-sensitive one.

questions.question: A company to which Section 135 applies must spend on CSR at least

options.A: two per cent of the turnover of the preceding year
options.B: five per cent of the net profit of the current year
options.C: two per cent of the average net profits of the preceding three financial years
options.D: ten per cent of the net worth

questions.explanation: The passage states the two per cent of three-year average net profit rule.

questions.question: Section 135 applies to a company which has, in the immediately preceding financial year,

options.A: paid-up capital of Rs 100 crore or more only
options.B: a net worth, turnover and net profit, each of Rs 500 crore or more
options.C: a net worth of Rs 500 crore or more, or turnover of Rs 1,000 crore or more, or net profit of Rs 5 crore or more
options.D: any three woman directors

questions.explanation: Any one of the three thresholds suffices.

questions.question: A company has unspent CSR funds relating to an ongoing project. It must

options.A: return the amount to shareholders as dividend
options.B: transfer the amount to an Unspent CSR Account within thirty days of the end of the financial year and spend it within three years
options.C: retain it in the general account without any time limit
options.D: transfer the amount to the Registrar immediately

questions.explanation: The passage states the rule for ongoing projects.

questions.question: On default in transferring unspent CSR funds, the company is liable to a penalty of

options.A: imprisonment of its directors for one year
options.B: the unspent amount or Rs 10 crore, whichever is more
options.C: one-tenth of the unspent amount
options.D: twice the unspent amount or Rs 1 crore, whichever is less

questions.explanation: The passage states the penalty for the company.

questions.question: Section 166(2) is best understood as requiring directors to

options.A: act on the instructions of the majority shareholder in every case
options.B: consider the interests of creditors alone
options.C: act only for the maximisation of dividends for shareholders
options.D: act in good faith in the best interests of the company, its employees, shareholders, community and the environment

questions.explanation: The passage states the stakeholder-sensitive duty.

questions.question: A listed company with paid-up share capital of Rs 120 crore has an all-male board. On the passage, the company

options.A: is in breach only if it fails to file the BRSR
options.B: is compliant, since the requirement applies only to companies with turnover above Rs 1,000 crore
options.C: is in breach of Section 149(1), which requires at least one woman director
options.D: is compliant, since the requirement applies only to private companies

questions.explanation: A listed company falls within the prescribed classes required to have a woman director.

passages.title: Natural Resources, Federalism and the Constitutional Framework for the Environment
passages.passage: Environmental governance in India rests on a constitutional framework shaped by the 42nd Amendment (1976), which inserted Article 48A, directing the State to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard forests and wildlife, and Article 51A(g), making the protection of the environment a fundamental duty. That Amendment also moved forests and the protection of wild animals and birds to the Concurrent List (Entries 17A and 17B). Public health and sanitation, agriculture, water and land are State subjects, industries and mines are in the Union List subject to the limits of the relevant entries, and Entry 56 of the Union List allows Parliament to regulate inter-State rivers where it declares it expedient. Article 253 empowers Parliament to legislate for the whole or any part of India to implement an international treaty, agreement or decision, and the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 was enacted under it to give effect to the decisions of the 1972 Stockholm Conference. Article 39(b) directs the State to secure that the ownership and control of the material resources of the community are so distributed as best to subserve the common good. In Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (November 2024), a nine-judge Bench held, by majority, that not every privately owned resource is a 'material resource of the community' under Article 39(b), though some may be, depending on factors such as the nature of the resource, its impact on the well-being of the community, its scarcity and the consequences of its being held in private hands. In Re: Natural Resources Allocation (Special Reference No. 1 of 2012), the Court held that auction is not a constitutional requirement for every alienation of natural resources, the method depending on the nature of the resource and the object of the policy, but that any method must be fair, transparent and consistent with the public trust. In Manohar Lal Sharma v. Principal Secretary (2014), the Court held the allocation of coal blocks arbitrary and illegal and cancelled it, with a few exceptions.

questions.question: Parliament is empowered by Article 253 to

options.A: legislate for the whole or any part of India to implement an international treaty, agreement or decision
options.B: override the Constitution in order to implement a treaty
options.C: legislate only on matters in the Concurrent List
options.D: legislate on any State subject at any time

questions.explanation: The passage states the scope of Article 253.

questions.question: The 42nd Amendment moved which of the following subjects to the Concurrent List?

options.A: Public health and sanitation
options.B: Forests and the protection of wild animals and birds
options.C: Mines and minerals
options.D: Water and irrigation

questions.explanation: The passage identifies Entries 17A and 17B.

questions.question: In Property Owners Association (2024), the nine-judge Bench held that

options.A: all privately owned resources are material resources of the community
options.B: no privately owned resource can ever be a material resource of the community
options.C: Article 39(b) is unenforceable by the State
options.D: not every privately owned resource is a material resource of the community, though some may be, depending on specified factors

questions.explanation: The passage records the holding and the factors.

questions.question: According to the Special Reference of 2012, as described, the alienation of natural resources

options.A: may be by any method, however arbitrary
options.B: must always be by auction
options.C: is a matter wholly outside judicial review
options.D: need not always be by auction, but the method chosen must be fair, transparent and consistent with the public trust

questions.explanation: The passage states that auction is not constitutionally mandatory for every resource.

questions.question: A State enacts a law acquiring every privately owned mine within its territory, on the single premise that all private property is a material resource of the community under Article 39(b). In the light of the 2024 decision, the law is

options.A: invalid only because the State has not obtained the approval of the President
options.B: unassailable, since Article 39(b) applies to all property
options.C: valid because mines are in the Union List
options.D: open to challenge, since the premise is untenable and each resource must be tested against factors such as nature, scarcity and impact on the community

questions.explanation: The 2024 decision rejects the premise that all private resources fall within Article 39(b).

questions.question: Assertion (A): Parliament was competent to enact the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 although the environment is not separately listed as a legislative subject. Reason (R): Article 253 empowers Parliament to legislate to implement international decisions, and the Act gave effect to decisions of the 1972 Stockholm Conference. Which is correct?

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: R supplies the source of legislative power for the 1986 Act.

passages.title: Nuisance, Public Duty and Noise Pollution
passages.passage: Private nuisance is an unlawful interference with a person's use or enjoyment of land. Where the interference causes material damage to property, the locality in which the defendant acts is irrelevant, but where it causes only personal discomfort, the character of the locality is taken into account, as in St Helen's Smelting Co. v. Tipping (1865). A claimant of abnormal sensitivity cannot complain of an act which would not affect an ordinary person (Robinson v. Kilvert). A public nuisance, defined by Section 270 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, is an act which causes common injury, danger or annoyance to the public or to people in general; a private individual may sue in tort only if he suffers special damage, and Section 91 of the Code of Civil Procedure allows a suit by the Advocate-General, or by two or more persons with the leave of the court. A Magistrate may also, under what was Section 133 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, make a conditional order for the removal of a public nuisance. In Municipal Council, Ratlam v. Vardhichand (1980), Krishna Iyer J. held that a municipality cannot plead lack of funds to avoid its statutory duty to provide drains and sanitation, and that the section is a tool to enforce public duty. In Ushaben v. Bhagyalaxmi Chitra Mandir (1978), the Gujarat High Court held that the screening of a film allegedly hurting the plaintiffs' religious feelings did not give rise to an actionable wrong. In Church of God (Full Gospel) in India v. K.K.R. Majestic Colony Welfare Association (2000), the Supreme Court held that no religion prescribes the use of loudspeakers and that noise pollution violates Article 21; in In Re: Noise Pollution (2005), it held that the right to speech does not include a right to impose noise on captive listeners and that every person has a right to sleep. The Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000 prescribe ambient noise standards for different zones, prohibit the use of loudspeakers between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m. except in emergencies, and allow a State to permit their use until midnight on not more than fifteen days in a year on festive and cultural occasions.

questions.question: Under Section 91 of the Code of Civil Procedure, as described, a suit in respect of a public nuisance may be brought by

options.A: any single person without leave of the court
options.B: the municipality alone
options.C: the Magistrate on his own motion only
options.D: the Advocate-General, or by two or more persons with the leave of the court

questions.explanation: The passage states the persons who may sue under Section 91.

questions.question: According to St Helen's Smelting Co. v. Tipping, the locality of the defendant's activity

options.A: is never relevant
options.B: is irrelevant where there is material damage to property, but is relevant where only personal discomfort is caused
options.C: is relevant only where the plaintiff is abnormally sensitive
options.D: is always decisive

questions.explanation: The passage states the distinction.

questions.question: In Municipal Council, Ratlam v. Vardhichand, the Supreme Court held that

options.A: a municipality cannot plead lack of funds to avoid its statutory duty to provide drains and sanitation
options.B: a municipality is exempt from duties for want of funds
options.C: a Magistrate has no power to order removal of a public nuisance
options.D: nuisance can be remedied only by a civil suit

questions.explanation: The passage records the holding.

questions.question: In Church of God (Full Gospel), the Supreme Court held that

options.A: loudspeakers may be used at any hour with a licence
options.B: noise is a matter of private nuisance only
options.C: religious freedom permits unlimited use of loudspeakers
options.D: no religion prescribes the use of loudspeakers, and noise pollution violates Article 21

questions.explanation: The passage states both limbs.

questions.question: A State permits the use of loudspeakers until midnight on ten days in a year on festive occasions. Under the Noise Pollution Rules as described, this permission is

options.A: invalid, since loudspeakers are prohibited absolutely between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m.
options.B: invalid, since only the Central Government may permit use at night
options.C: within the State's power, since up to fifteen days in a year may be permitted until midnight
options.D: valid only if the Supreme Court sanctions each occasion

questions.explanation: The Rules allow relaxation until midnight for not more than fifteen days in a year.

questions.question: The decision in Ushaben v. Bhagyalaxmi Chitra Mandir stands for the proposition that

options.A: hurt to religious feelings by the screening of a film does not give rise to an actionable wrong in tort
options.B: the Magistrate must stop all films with religious themes
options.C: a film may be restrained wherever any person objects
options.D: any film hurting religious feelings is a nuisance

questions.explanation: The passage records the holding.

passages.title: Frustration, Force Majeure and Commercial Hardship
passages.passage: Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 provides that an agreement to do an act impossible in itself is void, and that a contract to do an act which, after the contract is made, becomes impossible or, by reason of some event which the promisor could not prevent, unlawful, becomes void when the act becomes impossible or unlawful. In Satyabrata Ghose v. Mugneeram Bangur & Co. (1954), the Supreme Court held that 'impossible' in Section 56 is not confined to physical or literal impossibility; it covers the case where an untoward event or change of circumstances totally upsets the very foundation upon which the parties rested their bargain, so that the object of the contract is frustrated. The Court also held that, where the contract itself makes provision for the happening of such an event, the matter is governed by the contract and Section 56 does not apply. In Alopi Parshad & Sons v. Union of India (1960), the Court held that a contract is not frustrated merely because performance has become more onerous or costly, since the parties must be taken to have foreseen the risks of trade. In Energy Watchdog v. Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (2017), power generators who had bid on the basis of imported coal sought relief when a foreign government's regulation raised the price of the coal; the Supreme Court held that the increase in cost did not amount to force majeure, which is to be construed strictly according to the terms of the contract, nor to frustration under Section 56, since the agreements were not rendered impossible. Section 65 provides that, when an agreement is discovered to be void or a contract becomes void, any person who has received an advantage under it must restore it or make compensation to the person from whom he received it. Section 73 awards compensation for loss naturally arising from breach, and the Specific Relief Act, 1963 provides remedies where compensation is inadequate.

questions.question: Under Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act, a contract which becomes impossible to perform after it is made

options.A: becomes void when the act becomes impossible or unlawful
options.B: is illegal and punishable
options.C: remains valid and enforceable
options.D: becomes voidable at the option of the promisee only

questions.explanation: The passage states the rule.

questions.question: According to Alopi Parshad, a contract is NOT frustrated merely because

options.A: the subject-matter has been destroyed
options.B: the foundation of the contract has been totally upset
options.C: performance has become more onerous or costly
options.D: performance has become unlawful by a change in the law

questions.explanation: Mere hardship or increase in cost does not frustrate a contract.

questions.question: Where a contract contains an express provision for an event such as force majeure, Satyabrata Ghose holds that

options.A: the clause is void as against public policy
options.B: Section 56 overrides the contract
options.C: the matter is governed by the contract, and Section 56 does not apply
options.D: the court must disregard the clause

questions.explanation: The passage states this holding.

questions.question: Under Section 65, a person who has received an advantage under an agreement discovered to be void, or a contract which becomes void, must

options.A: pay a penalty to the State
options.B: retain it as damages
options.C: surrender it to the Registrar
options.D: restore it or make compensation to the person from whom he received it

questions.explanation: The passage states the obligation of restoration.

questions.question: A supplier agrees to supply goods at a fixed price using imported raw material. A foreign government's regulation sharply increases the import price, and the supplier claims that the contract is frustrated. On the basis of Energy Watchdog and Alopi Parshad, the claim is

options.A: certain to succeed, since the contract has become impossible
options.B: valid only if the supplier is a public sector body
options.C: certain to succeed, since the cause was a foreign regulation
options.D: unlikely to succeed, since an increase in cost alone does not amount to frustration or force majeure

questions.explanation: Increased cost does not make the contract impossible within Section 56.

questions.question: Assertion (A): Section 56 may apply even where performance remains physically possible. Reason (R): Satyabrata Ghose held that 'impossible' in Section 56 is not confined to physical impossibility, and covers the frustration of the foundation of the contract. Which is correct?

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: R states the holding which supports A.

passages.title: Traditional Knowledge, Biological Resources and Farmers' Rights
passages.passage: Indian law protects traditional knowledge and biological resources through several instruments. Section 3(p) of the Patents Act, 1970 excludes from patentability an invention which in effect is traditional knowledge or which is an aggregation or duplication of known properties of traditionally known components, and Section 25 permits opposition to a patent on the ground that the invention was anticipated by knowledge, oral or otherwise, available within any local or indigenous community in India or elsewhere. The Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL), set up in 2001, documents formulations from Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha and Yoga in languages and formats accessible to patent examiners worldwide, so as to prevent wrongful patents. Its precursors were successful challenges to the United States patent on the wound-healing use of turmeric, revoked in 1997 on a petition by the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research, and to the European patent on a neem-based fungicide, revoked in 2000 and upheld on appeal in 2005. The Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999 protects goods whose quality or reputation is attributable to their geographical origin, for ten years, renewable; Darjeeling tea was the first Indian product registered. The Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001 gives breeders exclusive rights in registered varieties, while Section 39(1)(iv) entitles a farmer to save, use, sow, resow, exchange, share or sell his farm produce, including seed of a protected variety, except that he may not sell branded seed. Section 6 of the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 requires the prior approval of the National Biodiversity Authority before an application for an intellectual property right is made on an invention based on research or information on a biological resource obtained from India. Together these provisions seek to balance incentives to innovate against the claims of communities who conserved the resources and developed the knowledge.

questions.question: The principal purpose of the Traditional Knowledge Digital Library is to

options.A: grant patents to traditional healers
options.B: regulate the export of medicinal plants
options.C: document traditional formulations in a form accessible to patent examiners, so as to prevent wrongful patents
options.D: register geographical indications for agricultural produce

questions.explanation: The passage states its purpose.

questions.question: Section 3(p) of the Patents Act, as described, excludes from patentability

options.A: an invention which in effect is traditional knowledge, or an aggregation or duplication of known properties of traditionally known components
options.B: every invention based on a plant
options.C: every pharmaceutical invention
options.D: any invention made by an Indian national

questions.explanation: The passage states the exclusion.

questions.question: Under Section 39(1)(iv) of the PPVFR Act, a farmer may

options.A: use seed of a protected variety only with the breeder's licence in every case
options.B: claim exclusive breeder's rights in registered varieties
options.C: sell branded seed of a protected variety freely
options.D: save, use, sow, resow, exchange, share or sell his farm produce including seed of a protected variety, but not sell branded seed

questions.explanation: The passage states the right and the exception for branded seed.

questions.question: Under Section 6 of the Biological Diversity Act, 2002, a person who wishes to apply for an intellectual property right on an invention based on a biological resource obtained from India must

options.A: obtain a no-objection certificate from the Patent Office alone
options.B: obtain the prior approval of the National Biodiversity Authority
options.C: pay a licence fee to the State Government
options.D: file the application first and seek approval afterwards

questions.explanation: The passage states the requirement of prior approval.

questions.question: A company applies for a patent on a herbal formulation identical to a classical Ayurvedic formulation documented in the TKDL. On the passage, the application

options.A: must be granted, since it is a new use in the market
options.B: is liable to be opposed as anticipated by traditional knowledge and as excluded under Section 3(p)
options.C: can be refused only on payment of a fee to the TKDL
options.D: can be refused only by the Biodiversity Authority

questions.explanation: Section 25 and Section 3(p) together apply to such formulations.

questions.question: Consider the following statements. 1. Darjeeling tea was the first Indian product registered under the Geographical Indications Act, 1999. 2. Under the PPVFR Act, a farmer may sell branded seed of a protected variety without restriction. 3. The United States patent on the wound-healing use of turmeric was revoked in 1997 on a petition by the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research. Which of the statements are correct?

options.A: 1 and 2 only
options.B: 1 and 3 only
options.C: 2 and 3 only
options.D: 1, 2 and 3

questions.explanation: Statements 1 and 3 are stated in the passage; branded seed may not be sold by a farmer.

passages.title: Forest Rights, Gram Sabhas and Sustainable Livelihoods
passages.passage: The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 (FRA) seeks to undo what it calls the historical injustice done to forest-dwelling communities. It recognises individual rights to hold and live in forest land under occupation, up to a ceiling of four hectares, and community rights, including the right to protect, regenerate, conserve or manage any community forest resource (Section 3(1)(i)). The Gram Sabha is the authority to initiate the process of determining rights (Section 6), assisted by a Forest Rights Committee, with appeals to the Sub-Divisional and District Level Committees. At least one-third of the members of the Committee must be women, and titles are to be registered jointly in the names of both spouses or, for a household headed by a single person, in the name of that person. Section 4(5) provides that no member of a forest-dwelling community shall be evicted or removed from forest land until the recognition and verification procedure is complete. Section 5 empowers the holders of rights and Gram Sabhas to protect wildlife, forests and biodiversity. In Samatha v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1997), the Supreme Court held that, in Scheduled Areas, the lease of tribal land to non-tribals for mining is void and that the State cannot grant mining leases to private persons, such activity being reserved to tribals, their cooperatives or State agencies. In Orissa Mining Corporation v. Ministry of Environment and Forests (the Niyamgiri case, 2013), the Court directed that Gram Sabhas decide whether the religious and cultural rights of the Dongria Kondh would be affected by bauxite mining, and the Gram Sabhas rejected the project. In 2022, the Forest (Conservation) Rules allowed the settlement of rights under the FRA to be completed after the in-principle approval of a forest diversion proposal, a change criticised as weakening community consent. The right to livelihood under Article 21, the Fifth Schedule and the Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 reinforce the position of Gram Sabhas.

questions.question: Under the FRA, the authority to initiate the process of determining forest rights is

options.A: the Gram Sabha
options.B: the Divisional Forest Officer
options.C: the National Green Tribunal
options.D: the District Collector alone

questions.explanation: Section 6 gives this role to the Gram Sabha.

questions.question: In the Niyamgiri case, the Supreme Court directed that

options.A: the Central Government alone decide on the mining project
options.B: Gram Sabhas decide whether the religious and cultural rights of the Dongria Kondh would be affected by the mining
options.C: the High Court appoint a committee of experts to decide all questions
options.D: the mining project be approved without further inquiry

questions.explanation: The passage records this direction.

questions.question: As regards the registration of titles under the FRA, the passage states that titles are to be

options.A: registered in the name of the Forest Department
options.B: registered in the name of the male head of the household only
options.C: registered only in the name of the Gram Sabha
options.D: registered jointly in the names of both spouses, or in the name of the single head of a household

questions.explanation: The passage describes joint titles, which also protect women's claims.

questions.question: Section 4(5) of the FRA provides that no forest dweller shall be evicted from forest land

options.A: unless the occupation exceeds four hectares
options.B: without the order of the Supreme Court in every case
options.C: unless the Forest Department so decides
options.D: until the recognition and verification procedure is complete

questions.explanation: The passage states the protection.

questions.question: A State grants a mining lease over tribal land in a Scheduled Area to a private company. On the basis of Samatha, the lease is

options.A: void, since in Scheduled Areas such mining is reserved to tribals, their cooperatives or State agencies
options.B: valid if the Gram Sabha is informed afterwards
options.C: valid, since the State owns all minerals
options.D: valid if the company pays compensation

questions.explanation: Samatha held such leases to private persons void.

questions.question: Assertion (A): The FRA treats forest-dwelling communities not only as holders of rights but also as custodians of forests and biodiversity. Reason (R): Section 5 empowers the holders of forest rights and Gram Sabhas to protect wildlife, forests and biodiversity. Which is correct?

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: Section 5 gives statutory expression to the custodial role asserted in A.
